claims.assertion: The trip was metered (RydeTAXI), so every extra kilometre driven enters the fare: the records show 24.7 km actual against 21.6 km optimal, +3.2 km (+15%), and $4.45 was billed as excess distance at $1.41/km.

One off-route segment is recorded, 23:06–23:12, 2.96 km driven where the optimal route covers 0.00 km, reaching up to 974 m from the optimal route — a deviation with extra mileage that must be reviewed under RD-3/RD-4/RD-5 and refunded if not exempt.

The driver cannot claim the 'reasonable cause' exemption for congestion: the only traffic facts are speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard, and band 4 is neither a band 1 nor band 2 record, so it fails RD-4(b) and cannot exempt the segment.
No traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, and weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain, so the RD-4(a) incident exemption and any weather-based justification are unavailable.

The driver's 'traffic building up' statement and his chat request do not substitute for traffic evidence: RD-4 requires traffic facts for the substituted optimal stretch, and the system traffic records show only mid-band speeds and no incident.

The rider's agreement at 23:03 ('Sure, go ahead') was given without any named location — the driver had not disclosed the Bedok South Avenue 3 detour point — and the off-route segment began at 23:06, so the consent did not cover the route change to a place the rider never specified; the segment is not exempt.

The refund is computable from fare facts: only the mileage units are refunded, i.e. the 2.96 km of the unexempted segment at the trip's per-km rate of $1.41 ($34.84 ÷ 24.7 km), rounded to the cent = $4.17 rent, while the map-matching residual (3.2 km − 2.96 km = 0.24 km, ≤ 0.25 km) is not refunded.
The driver's 90-day record shows 0 upheld route disputes, so the repeated-offence condition for an account flag is not met and no flag_account is requested on this case.

weaknesses: The rider expressly agreed to the reroute in chat (F8, 'Sure, go ahead') one minute after the driver's request (F7) and three minutes before the off-route segment started (F3) — the driver will argue RD-5 pre-departure agreement, and the policy text arguably does not require him to name the exact road.

The driver's stated reason is traffic (F9), and the traffic records do show mid-level congestion (F10 band 4 on ECP, F11), which the driver will present as a reasonable cause despite RD-4(b) making band evidence only corroborative and never sufficient alone.
The rider's own profile shows 4 disputes in 90 days with 2 upheld (F14), which the driver's side may use to suggest a pattern of fare complaints rather than a genuine one-off overcharge.

claims.assertion: The only off-route segment on the trip is F3 (23:06–23:12, 2.96 km added), and it was agreed with the rider in advance: at 23:03 the driver proposed 'go round via Bedok South Avenue 3' (F7) and the rider replied 'Sure, go ahead' (F8) — three minutes before that segment started at 23:06.

The rider's agreement expressly named the reroute via Bedok South Avenue 3, so it covers this exact segment and not merely a generic 'stop' request; the consent therefore exempts the segment under RD-5 (the driver also recorded the same sequence in his statement, F9).

The driver had a genuine traffic reason for the reroute: East Coast Parkway was running at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) throughout 22:32–23:35 (F10), which is the road he was avoiding; no incident was logged, so this is corridor congestion (F12), and the reroute was taken to keep the trip efficient.

Because the agreed-and-congestion-justified segment is exempt, there is no unexempted off-route segment under RD-1, so the metered overshoot the rider complains of ($4.45 for 3.2 km billed, F4, within the $53.17 total in F6) is the honest metered consequence of the accepted route and attracts no refund under RD-2.

Only 2.96 km of the 3.2 km excess is attributable to the one off-route segment (F3 vs F1), and that entire amount is the consented segment; the balance is map-matching residue, which RD-2 expressly does not refund even for a non-exempt segment.

The driver's record is consistent with a compliant trip: 4.0-year account, 4.7 rating, 1199 trips in 90 days and 1 dispute with 0 upheld (F15), so no flag_account under RD-6 is warranted — the profile shows no prior upheld route dispute.

The longer duration (49.8 min vs 28 min estimate, F2) does not create a separate refundable item: time is charged at the taxi meter on the actual route and the rider's own agreement to the detour plus corridor congestion at band 4 (F10) explains the extra minutes, not a discretionary overcharge.

weaknesses: The system record shows a real 2.96 km off-route segment (F3) and a 49.8-minute trip versus a 28-minute estimate (F2) — the rider will lead with F1/F2 to argue the ride took materially longer and cost more than quoted.

The traffic record the rider will use cuts both ways: F10 shows band 4 (30–39 km/h), which is congestion but not band 1/2, and under RD-4(b) a band record alone does not exempt a segment — so the driver's traffic excuse rests entirely on the RD-5 consent in F8, not on RD-4.
There is no traffic incident at all (F12), so RD-4(a) is unavailable; the driver cannot claim a road closure, accident or blockage forced the detour.

The rider's 90-day profile shows 2 upheld route disputes (F14), which the rider may use to argue this is a pattern; the driver must rely on the pre-23:06 timing of F7/F8 to distinguish this consented reroute.

points.response: The 23:03 exchange (F7/F8) does precede the segment start at 23:06 (F3), but RD-5 exempts only the route change the rider actually agreed to; the driver's message named a general corridor without disclosing the detour point that produced the off-route segment, so the timing alone does not carry the exemption.

The message named a road, not the deviation: RD-3(b) withholds exemption where the driver chose a point producing an off-route segment without telling the passenger that location beforehand, and the record shows the rider was never told the detour went up to 974 m off the optimal route (F3, F8).

Band 4 at 30–39 km/h (F10) is neither band 1 nor band 2, so it is at most corroboration and never a standalone exemption under RD-4(b), and with no incident logged (F12) the driver has no RD-4(a) evidence aimed at the replaced stretch of the optimal route.

Because the RD-5/RD-4 exemptions fail, the 2.96 km segment stays unexempted under RD-1 and the metered extra distance is refundable: fare facts show $4.45 billed as 3.2 km at $1.41/km inside the $53.17 total (F4, F6), and the refund is the segment's own mileage.

I agree the 0.24 km residual (3.2 km actual minus 2.96 km segment, ≤ 0.25 km) is map-matching noise that RD-2 does not refund — but that leaves the full 2.96 km segment refundable at the trip's $1.41/km, i.e. $4.17, not $0.
The rider does not seek a flag_account: the driver's 90-day profile shows 0 upheld route disputes (F15), so RD-6's repeated-violation condition is not met and this exchange drops out of the case.

Duration is charged by the meter and is not a separate refundable item, so I do not claim it; F2 is cited only as context, and the refund rests solely on the unexempted segment's extra kilometres under RD-2.

The metered arithmetic is not in dispute (F1, F4, F6), but RD-2 only refunds mileage on an *unexempted* off-route segment, and here the sole segment is exempt under RD-5, so no portion of the $4.45 excess is refundable.
